newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Focus-Low offers for India's term diesel tender.
newsitem.headline: Focus-Low offers for India's term diesel tender.

text.p: Unexpectedly low offers were seen in the Indian Oil Corp's (IOC) term tender for the purchase of 1.0 percent sulphur high speed diesel for delivery from June 1997 to May 1998, industry sources said on Friday.

Traders said the lowest offer came from a Japanese trader for the delivery of 140,000 tonnes to Kandla on the west coast at 68 cents per tonne over Middle East quotes, on a cost-and-freight basis (c-and-f).

Next was from a Middle East producer for the delivery of 80,000 tonnes at around 90 cents premium with the same Japanese trader offering at about 6 cents above this for 87,000 tonne cargoes, both above MidEast quotes on a c-and-f basis.
Low offers were also seen for the normal 45,000-tonne lots which were heard at around $2.00 premium c-and-f Kandla, about 50 cents below last year's awarded price.
Industry sources said the low offers were due to market perception that supplies will exceed demand over the next 12 months caused by capacity expansions in Asia and the Middle East.
"The numbers (premiums) just cover the freight costs, in some cases even that is not covered. These people are taking the long term view that the market will be in surplus," said a trader.
Another trader said the low offers from the Japanese trader maybe due to the company's decision to be more actively involved in the Indian energy sector.
"Some Japanese companies want the volume and they may not be too concerned with the profitability of the deal. If they make money from seven out of 12 of the cargoes, that its okay," the trader said.
"They may also have some plans for other developments in India."
The Japanese trader's low offer was also partly put down to its easy access to a large tanker fleet through its close ties with one company and small stake in another trading company.
Both of these companies have large tanker fleets.
But other traders cautioned that IOC might not take all the big cargoes that were offered at the low levels as it will cause major logistical problems.
"I don't think IOC can take two large cargoes in the same area," said a trader.
The large cargoes will have to be lightered to smaller coastal tankers for final shipment to Kandla, he said.
Traders also noticed that the offers were not exactly in line with the IOC tender requirement.
IOC had requested for 12 cargoes each of either 87,000 tonnes or 130,000 tonnes but two of the offers were for 80,000 tonnes and 140,000 tonnes.
"IOC will need to resolve the volume issue," said a trader.
Most industry sources said that IOC is very likely to take only one of the large cargoes offered.

In its last one-year term tender, IOC bought three 0.5 percent sulphur cargoes of 45,000 tonne each from western trading house Cargill, Swiss trader Glencore and Dutch trader Vitol at premiums of between $2.49-2.59 per barrel on a c-and-f basis to Kandla.
Traders said the offers for the 0.25 percent sulphur diesel was at a premium of under $2.00 for delivery to Kandla to the west coast.
Offers to the east cost was heard at a low of $1.45 premium while other offers were made at 30 cents premium to MidEast quotes on a free-on-board Kuwait basis, all for 45,000 tonne lots.
The offers to IOC's tender to buy kerosene were not far off last year's awarded price at around $1.40 premium for the west coast and around $2.00 for the east coast.
In its previous tender, IOC bought one cargo at $1.34 premium for delivery to the west coast and another at $1.90 premium to the east coast.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3093)
